raw_text:
# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 60 million people worldwide and carrying substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs [1]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a large proportion of patients remain symptomatic [2]. Notably, CRT is only indicated in patients with prolonged QRS duration, leaving the majority of HF patients with narrow QRS without an effective device option [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) therapy has emerged as a device-based approach designed to improve contractility and symptoms in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction, particularly those with narrow QRS complexes [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM delivers non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac action potential [5]. Because these high-voltage signals (~7.5 V) are timed to coincide with myocardial depolarization, they do not trigger an additional contraction but instead modulate the strength of the existing contraction [6]. The proposed mechanisms include enhanced calcium handling through upregulation of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA2a) and normalization of phospholamban activity [7]. Preclinical studies have demonstrated reversal of the fetal gene program and improvements in proteins regulating calcium cycling and cellular signaling [8]. These molecular effects suggest that CCM may favorably influence pathological myocardial remodeling beyond acute hemodynamic improvement [9].

## Clinical Evidence

The clinical development of CCM has spanned multiple randomized controlled trials. The FIX-HF-4 study, a crossover trial, demonstrated improvements in peak oxygen consumption (VO2) and quality of life, though a placebo effect was noted given the crossover design [10]. The FIX-HF-5 trial evaluated CCM in patients with NYHA class III–IV HF and ejection fraction ≤35% [11]. While the primary endpoint of anaerobic threshold was not met across the entire cohort, a prespecified subgroup analysis identified patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% as deriving the greatest benefit [12]. This led to the FIX-HF-5C study, which confirmed significant improvements in peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, and quality of life as measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire [13].

A pooled analysis of individual patient data from randomized trials further supported improvements in exercise tolerance and functional status [14]. The FIX-HF-5C2 study, using a refined two-lead system, demonstrated comparable efficacy with a simplified implantation approach [15]. Long-term registry data, including the CCM-REG study, have shown sustained improvements in NYHA class and suggested reductions in HF hospitalizations [16]. Importantly, several analyses have suggested a particularly favorable effect in patients with ejection fractions in the higher range of HFrEF [17].

## Patient Selection and Safety

Current indications for CCM, including U.S. FDA approval, target patients with NYHA class III HF, ejection fraction between 25% and 45%, narrow QRS (<130 ms), and persistent symptoms despite GDMT [18]. The therapy is delivered by the Optimizer system, an implantable pulse generator that requires periodic recharging [19]. Safety analyses across trials have demonstrated an acceptable profile, with no significant increase in arrhythmias or mortality [20]. The device does not interfere with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators when appropriately programmed, allowing concomitant use in patients requiring both therapies [21].

## Emerging Applications and Limitations

Interest has grown in extending CCM to patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), where therapeutic options remain limited [22]. Early studies and ongoing trials are investigating its role in this population, given the potential effects on diastolic function and exercise capacity [23]. CCM has also been studied in patients with atrial fibrillation, who were excluded from many earlier trials, with promising preliminary results [24].

Despite encouraging functional outcomes, important limitations remain. No adequately powered trial has demonstrated a mortality benefit, and most evidence derives from studies with relatively small sample sizes [25]. The need for device recharging and the costs associated with implantation may limit broader adoption [26]. Furthermore, the placebo effect inherent in device trials complicates interpretation of symptomatic endpoints [27].

## Conclusion

CCM represents a valuable addition to the device-based armamentarium for HF, particularly for patients with narrow QRS who are ineligible for CRT [28]. Robust evidence supports improvements in exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life [29]. However, definitive demonstration of mortality benefit and clarification of its role in HFpEF and atrial fibrillation await ongoing and future randomized trials [30]. As experience accumulates, CCM may become an increasingly important option for the substantial population of HF patients with persistent symptoms despite optimal therapy.
